content: Cefprozil is a second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating mild to moderate infections of the upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract, and uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections. Common adverse reactions include diarrhea, nausea, elevated ALT/SGPT and AST/SGOT levels, and vaginitis. Adult Indications and Dosage Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis: Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Dosage: 500 mg daily for 10 days. Otitis Media: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Dosage: 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. Acute Sinusitis: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Dosage: 250 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. Secondary Bacterial Infections of Acute Bronchitis and Acute Bacterial Exacerbation of Chronic Bronchitis: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase-producing strains), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase-producing strains). Dosage: 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. Skin and Skin-Structure Infections: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including penicillinase-producing strains) and Streptococcus pyogenes. Abscesses may require surgical drainage. Dosage: 250 mg every 12 hours for 10 days, or 500 mg daily for 10 days, or 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. Contraindications Cefprozil is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporin antibiotics. Warnings Before initiating therapy, assess for previous hypersensitivity reactions to cefprozil, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-sensitivity among β-lactam antibiotics is documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue the drug immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefprozil. CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinue ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile and initiate appropriate treatment. Adverse Reactions Gastrointestinal: Diarrhea (2%), nausea (1%), vomiting (1%), abdominal pain (1%). Hepatic: Rare cases of cholestatic jaundice have been reported. Central Nervous System: Dizziness (1%), rare reports of hyperactivity, headache, nervousness, insomnia, confusion, and somnolence (<1%), all reversible. Hematologic: Rare reports of aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, hemorrhage, prolonged prothrombin time, and positive Coombs’ test. Renal: Rare reports of renal dysfunction and toxic nephropathy. Dermatologic: Rare cases of toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Seizures: Cephalosporins, including cefprozil, have been implicated in triggering seizures, particularly in patients with renal impairment when dosage adjustments were not made. Drug Interactions Nephrotoxicity has been reported with concurrent use of aminoglycoside antibiotics and cephalosporins. Probenecid doubles the area under the curve (AUC) for cefprozil. The bioavailability of cefprozil is not affected by antacids. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Animal studies have shown no harm to the fetus, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Lactation: Cefprozil is excreted in human milk in small amounts. Caution is advised when administering to nursing women. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy are established for otitis media (6 months to 12 years), pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and uncomplicated skin infections (2 to 12 years). Not established for children under 6 months for otitis media or acute sinusitis, or under 2 years for pharyngitis/tonsillitis or skin infections. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies show no significant differences in safety or efficacy between elderly and younger patients. However, elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, necessitating careful dose selection and monitoring of renal function. Renal Impairment: Dosage reduction is recommended due to the risk of high or prolonged plasma antibiotic concentrations. Hepatic Impairment: The half-life of cefprozil increases to approximately 2 hours, but no dosage adjustment is necessary. Administration and Monitoring Administer orally. Limited information is available regarding monitoring parameters for cefprozil. Overdosage High doses in animal studies caused no mortality or significant toxicity. In cases of severe overdose, particularly in patients with renal impairment, hemodialysis can aid in drug removal. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Cefprozil inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, leading to bactericidal activity. Pharmacokinetics: Approximately 95% of the dose is absorbed following oral administration. Plasma protein binding is approximately 36%. No accumulation occurs in individuals with normal renal function. Patient Counseling Patients should be informed that cefprozil is only effective against bacterial infections and should not be used for viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Emphasize the importance of completing the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if symptoms improve early, to prevent treatment failure and resistance development. Diarrhea is a common side effect and usually resolves after discontinuation of the antibiotic. However, if watery or bloody stools occur, even up to two months after the last dose, patients should contact their physician immediately. Storage Store at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Brand Name Cefzil.
